what_it_does: On-device training and inference of neural networks on edge devices (like phones) requires specialized hardware because neural network operations are data-intensive. This paper describes a chip built at 28 nanometers that combines SRAM (the fast, on-chip memory) with processing circuits for neural-network math (compute-in-memory, or CIM). The key innovation is a 'dual-mode transpose' architecture that uses the same circuits for both feedforward (the normal forward pass through the network) and backpropagation (the backward pass that learns by adjusting weights). Typically, separate circuits handle these two directions, wasting silicon area; here, a single set of math units handles both by transposing weight matrices. The design uses floating-point numbers (which preserve accuracy better than integer rounding) and includes an 'approximate mode' that trades a tiny bit of accuracy for higher speed and lower power when speed matters more than precision. This enables both training and inference on a tiny chip — achieving 192.3 trillion floating-point operations per watt of power.
